'''Dyscalculia''' is a [[Learning disability|learning disorder]], resulting in difficulty learning or comprehending [[arithmetic]], such as difficulty in understanding [[number]]s, [[numeracy]], learning how to manipulate numbers, performing mathematical calculations, and learning facts in mathematics. In the United Kingdom it is classified as a specific learning difficulty. It is sometimes colloquially referred to as "math [[dyslexia]]."<ref>{{cite web |title=Dyscalculia |url=https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/23949-dyscalculia |website=Cleveland Clinic |access-date=11 September 2026}}</ref>

Dyscalculia is associated with dysfunction in the region around the [[intraparietal sulcus]],<ref name=":1" /> and potentially also the [[frontal lobe]].<ref name="Shalev" /><ref name="Rubinsten2009" /> Dyscalculia does not reflect a general deficit in cognitive abilities or difficulties with time, measurement, and [[Spatial visualization ability|spatial reasoning]].<ref name = "Butterworth, 2010">{{cite journal |last= Butterworth |first= B | year = 2010 | title = Foundational numerical capacities and the origins of dyscalculia |journal = Trends in Cognitive Sciences | volume = 14 | issue = 12 | pages = 534–541 | pmid = 20971676 | doi = 10.1016/j.tics.2010.09.007|s2cid= 13590517 }}</ref><ref name = "Butterworth, 2011">{{cite journal |last1= Butterworth |first1= B |last2= Varma |first2= S |last3= Laurillard |first3= D | year = 2011 | title = Dyscalculia: From brain to education | journal = [[Science (journal)|Science]] | volume = 332 | issue = 6033 | pages = 1049–1053 | pmid = 21617068 | doi = 10.1126/science.1201536|bibcode= 2011Sci...332.1049B |s2cid= 13311738 }}</ref> Estimates of the prevalence of dyscalculia range between three and six percent of the population.<ref name = "Butterworth, 2010" /><ref name = "Butterworth, 2011" />

In 2015, it was established that 11% of children with dyscalculia also have [[attention deficit hyperactivity disorder]] (ADHD).<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Soares |first1=Neelkamal |last2=Patel |first2=Dilip R. |year=2015 |title=Dyscalculia |journal=International Journal of Child and Adolescent Health |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=15–26}}</ref> Dyscalculia has also been associated with [[Turner syndrome]],<ref>{{citation|title=The Learning Brain: Memory and Brain Development in Children|first=Torkel|last=Klingberg|publisher= [[Oxford University Press]] |year=2013|isbn=978-0-19-991710-5|page= 68|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=SIqOLf3lnNYC&pg=PA68}}</ref> [[Down syndrome]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cuskelly |first1=Monica |last2=Faragher |first2=Rhonda |date=2019-03-04 |title=Developmental Dyscalculia and Down Syndrome: Indicative Evidence |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/1034912X.2019.1569209 |journal=International Journal of Disability, Development and Education |language=en |volume=66 |issue=2 |pages=151–161 |doi=10.1080/1034912X.2019.1569209 |issn=1034-912X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and people who have [[spina bifida]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barnes |first1=Marcia A. |last2=Wilkinson |first2=Margaret |last3=Khemani |first3=Ekta |last4=Boudesquie |first4=Amy |last5=Dennis |first5=Maureen |last6=Fletcher |first6=Jack M. |date=March 2006 |title=Arithmetic processing in children with spina bifida: Calculation accuracy, strategy use, and fact retrieval fluency |journal=Journal of Learning Disabilities |volume=39 |issue=2 |pages=174–187 |doi=10.1177/00222194060390020601 |issn=0022-2194 |pmid=16583797|s2cid=18981877 }}</ref>

==Signs and symptoms==
The earliest appearance of dyscalculia is typically a deficit in [[subitizing]], which is the ability to know, from a brief glance and without counting, how many objects there are in a small group. Children as young as five can subitize six objects, especially while looking at the dots on the sides of [[dice]]; however, children with dyscalculia can subitize fewer objects and, even when correct, take longer to identify the number than their age-matched peers.<ref>{{cite journal | title = Subitizing and visual counting in children with problems in acquiring basic arithmetic skills | journal = Optometry & Vision Development | year = 2008 | first1 = B | last1 = Fischer | first2 = C | last2 = Gebhardt | first3 = K | last3 = Hartnegg | volume = 39 | issue = 1 | pages = 24–9 | url = http://www.lookingforlearning.com/abstracts/ovd39-1.pdf | access-date = 11 June 2013 | archive-date = 9 October 2010 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20101009122555/http://lookingforlearning.com/abstracts/ovd39-1.pdf }}</ref>

Dyscalculia often looks different at different ages. It tends to become more apparent as children get older; however, symptoms can appear as early as preschool.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-08-05 |title=What Is Dyscalculia |url=https://www.understood.org/en/articles/what-is-dyscalculia |access-date=2023-04-07 |website=Understood |language=en}}</ref> Common symptoms of dyscalculia are having difficulty with [[mental calculation]], trouble analyzing time and reading an analog clock, struggle with motor sequencing that involves numbers, and often counting on fingers when adding numbers.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Frye |first=Devon |date=2017-02-15 |title=What Does Dyscalculia Look Like in Adults? |language=en-US |work=ADDitude |url=https://www.additudemag.com/dyscalculia-in-adults-symptoms-signs-and-statistics/ |access-date=2018-05-02}}</ref>

===Persistence in children===
Although many researchers believe dyscalculia to be a persistent disorder, evidence on the persistence of dyscalculia remains mixed.<ref name=pmid25529864>{{cite journal|vauthors=Kucian K, von Aster M|title=Developmental Dyscalculia |journal=European Journal of Pediatrics|date=2015|volume=174|issue=1|pages=1–13 |doi=10.1007/s00431-014-2455-7 |pmid=25529864|s2cid=206987063 |url=https://www.zora.uzh.ch/id/eprint/104168/1/ZORA_NL_104168.pdf }}</ref> For instance, in a study done by Mazzocco and Myers (2003), researchers evaluated children on a slew of measures and selected their most consistent measure as their best diagnostic criterion: a stringent 10th-percentile cut-off on the TEMA-2.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Mozzocco|last2=Myers|title=Complexities in identifying and defining mathematics learning disability in the primary school-age years|journal=Annals of Dyslexia|date=2003|volume=53|issue=1|pages=218–253|doi=10.1007/s11881-003-0011-7|pmid=19750132|pmc=2742419}}</ref> Even with their best criterion, they found dyscalculia diagnoses for children longitudinally did not persist; only 65% of students who were ever diagnosed over the course of four years were diagnosed for at least two years. The percentage of children who were diagnosed in two consecutive years was further reduced. It is unclear whether this was the result of misdiagnosed children improving in mathematics and spatial awareness as they progressed as normal, or that the subjects who showed improvement were accurately diagnosed, but exhibited signs of a non-persistent learning disability.{{Citation needed|date=July 2021}}{{original research inline|date=October 2025}}

=== Persistence in adults ===
There are very few studies of adults with dyscalculia who have had a history of it growing up, but such studies have shown that it can persist into adulthood. It can affect major parts of an adult's life.<ref>{{Cite journal |author1=Attout, Lucie |author2=Salmon, Eric |author3=Majerus, Steve |date=2015 |title=Working Memory for Serial Order Is Dysfunctional in Adults With a History of Developmental Dyscalculia: Evidence From Behavioral and Neuroimaging Data |journal=Developmental Neuropsychology |volume=40 |issue=4 |pages=230–47 |doi=10.1080/87565641.2015.1036993|pmid=26179489 |s2cid=33166929 }}</ref> Most adults with dyscalculia have a hard time processing mathematics at a 4th-grade level. For 1st–4th grade level, many adults will know what to do for the mathematics problem, but they will often get them wrong because of "careless errors", although they are not careless when it comes to the problem.<ref name=":2" />

The adults cannot process their errors on the problems or may not even recognize that they have made these errors. Visual-spatial input, auditory input, and touch input will be affected due to these processing errors. Dyscalculics may experience difficulties when adding numbers in a column format. Their mind can mix up the numbers, and it is possible that they may get the same (wrong) answer twice due to their mind processing the problem incorrectly. Dyscalculics can have problems determining differences in different coins and their size or giving the correct amount of change and if numbers are grouped together, it is possible that they cannot determine which has less or more.<ref name=":2" />

Dyscalculics are slower and make more mistakes when asked to choose the greater of two numbers, especially when those numbers are close together.<ref name=pmid23302840>{{Cite journal|last=Callaway|first=Ewen|date=2013-01-09 |title=Dyscalculia: Number games |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=493 |issue=7431 |pages=150–153 |doi=10.1038/493150a |pmid=23302840 |issn=0028-0836 |bibcode=2013Natur.493..150C|doi-access=free }}</ref> Research has also documented impaired visuo-spatial statistical 
learning in adults with dyscalculia. 
<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Levy |first1=Sarit 
|last2=Turk-Browne |first2=Nicholas B. |last3=Goldfarb 
|first3=Liat |title=Impaired visuo-spatial statistical learning with mathematical learning difficulties |journal=Visual Cognition 
|date=2023 |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=138–148 
|doi=10.1080/13506285.2023.2176168 
|doi-broken-date=8 April 2026 
}}</ref> Adults with dyscalculia may struggle with directions while driving and with controlling their finances, leading to difficulties on a day-to-day basis.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.additudemag.com/dyscalculia-in-adults-symptoms-signs-and-statistics/ |title=What Does Dyscalculia Look Like in Adults?|last=Frye|first=Devon|date=2017-02-15 |work=ADDitude |access-date=2018-04-25|language=en-US}}</ref>

====College students or other adult learners====
College students particularly may have a difficult time due to the fast pace and change in difficulty of the work they are given. As a result of this, students may develop much anxiety and frustration. After dealing with their anxiety for a long time, students can become averse to mathematics and try to avoid it as much as possible, which may result in lower grades in mathematics courses. Students with dyscalculia, however, can also do exceptionally well in writing, reading, and speaking.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|title=College & Dyscalculia|url=https://www.dyscalculia.org/college-dyscalculia|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210709072310/https://www.dyscalculia.org/college-dyscalculia|archive-date=2021-07-09|access-date=2021-07-09|website=www.dyscalculia.org|language=en-US}}</ref>

==Causes==
Both [[domain-general learning|domain-general]] and [[domain-specific]] causes have been put forth. With respect to pure developmental dyscalculia, domain-general causes are unlikely as they should not impair one's ability in the numerical domain without also affecting other domains such as reading.{{citation needed|date=July 2021}} In favor of domain-general theories, some studies suggested that some other cognitive functions as spatial skills, [[face perception]] and general working memory could be a predictor of dyscalculia and comorbid dyslexia/dyscalculia.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Peters |first1=Lien |last2=Op de Beeck |first2=Hans |last3=De Smedt |first3=Bert |date=December 2020 |title=Cognitive correlates of dyslexia, dyscalculia and comorbid dyslexia/dyscalculia: Effects of numerical magnitude processing and phonological processing |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0891422220302389 |journal=Research in Developmental Disabilities |language=en |volume=107 |article-number=103806 |doi=10.1016/j.ridd.2020.103806|pmid=33152663 |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Grant |first1=Jeremy G. |last2=Siegel |first2=Linda S. |last3=D'Angiulli |first3=Amedeo |date=2020-10-22 |title=From Schools to Scans: A Neuroeducational Approach to Comorbid Math and Reading Disabilities |journal=Frontiers in Public Health |volume=8 |article-number=469 |doi=10.3389/fpubh.2020.00469 |doi-access=free |issn=2296-2565 |pmc=7642246 |pmid=33194932|bibcode=2020FrPH....8..469G }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baulina |first1=Maria |last2=Kosonogov |first2=Vladimir |date=2024-01-03 |title="Calculating faces": can face perception paradigms enrich dyscalculia research? |journal=Frontiers in Psychology |language=English |volume=14 |article-number=1218124 |doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1218124 |doi-access=free |pmid=38235284 |pmc=10791763 |issn=1664-1078}}</ref> Two competing domain-specific hypotheses about the causes of developmental dyscalculia have been proposed – the ''magnitude representation'' (or ''number module deficit hypothesis'') and the ''access deficit hypothesis''.{{citation needed|date=July 2021}}

===Magnitude representation deficit===
[[File:Gray726 parietal lobe.png|thumb|upright=1.4|The part of the brain where the [[Sulcus (neuroanatomy)|sulcus]] is located in the [[parietal lobe]].]]
Dehaene's "[[number sense]]" theory suggests that approximate numerosities are automatically ordered in an ascending manner on a mental number line.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Dehaene|first1=S.|title=Precis of the number sense|journal=Mind & Language|date=2001|volume=16|issue=1|pages=16–36|doi=10.1111/1468-0017.00154}}</ref> The mechanism to represent and process non-symbolic magnitude (e.g., number of dots) is often known as the "[[approximate number system]]" (ANS), and a core deficit in the precision of the ANS, known as the "magnitude representation hypothesis" or "number module deficit hypothesis", has been proposed as an underlying cause of developmental dyscalculia.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Butterworth |first=B. |title=Handbook of mathematical cognition |publisher=[[Psychology Press]] |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-203-99804-5 |editor-last=Campbell |editor-first=Jamie I. D. |location=Hove, UK |pages=455–467 |chapter=Developmental dyscalculia}}</ref>

In particular, the structural features of the ANS are theoretically supported by a phenomenon called the "numerical distance effect", which has been robustly observed in numerical comparison tasks.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Moyer|first1=R. S.|last2=Landauer|first2=T. K.|title=Time required for judgements of numerical inequality|journal=Nature|date=1967|volume=215|issue=5109|pages=1519–1520|doi=10.1038/2151519a0|pmid=6052760|bibcode=1967Natur.215.1519M|s2cid=4298073}}</ref> Typically developing individuals are less accurate and slower in comparing pairs of numbers closer together (e.g., 7 and 8) than further apart (e.g., 2 and 9). A related "numerical ratio effect" (in which the ratio between two numbers varies but the distance is kept constant, e.g., 2 vs. 5 and 4 vs. 7) based on [[Weber–Fechner law|Weber's law]] has also been used to further support the structure of the ANS.<ref name=Halberda2008>{{cite journal|last1=Halberda|first1=J.|last2=Mazzocco|first2=M. M. M.|last3=Feigenson|first3=L.|title=Individual differences in non-verbal number acuity correlate with maths achievement|journal=Nature|date=2008|volume=455|issue=7213|pages=665–668|doi=10.1038/nature07246|pmid=18776888|bibcode=2008Natur.455..665H|s2cid=27196030}}</ref>

The numerical ratio effect is observed when individuals are less accurate and slower in comparing pairs of numbers that have a larger ratio (e.g., 8 and 9, ratio = 8/9) than a smaller ratio (2 and 3; ratio = 2/3). A larger numerical distance or ratio effect with comparison of sets of objects (i.e., non-symbolic) is thought to reflect a less precise ANS, and ANS acuity has been found to correlate with mathematical achievement in typically developing children,<ref name=Halberda2008 /> as well as in adults.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Halberda|first1=J.|last2=Ly|first2=R.|last3=Wilmer|first3=J. B.|last4=Naiman|first4=D. Q.|last5=Germine|first5=L.|title=Number sense across the lifespan as revealed by a massive Internet-based sample|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|date=2012|volume=109|issue=28|pages=11116–11120|doi=10.1073/pnas.1200196109|bibcode=2012PNAS..10911116H|pmid=22733748|pmc=3396479|doi-access=free}}</ref>

More importantly, several behavioral studies have found that children with developmental dyscalculia show an attenuated distance/ratio effect compared with typically developing children. Neuroimaging studies have provided additional insights even when behavioral difference in distance/ratio effect might not be clearly evident.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Ashkenazi|first1=S.|last2=Mark-Zigdon|first2=N.|last3=Henik|first3=A.|title=Numerical distance effect in developmental dyscalculia|journal=Cognitive Development|date=2009|volume=24|issue=4|pages=387–400|doi=10.1016/j.cogdev.2009.09.006}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Mussolin|first1=C.|last2=Mejias|first2=S.|last3=Noël|first3=M. P.|title=Symbolic and nonsymbolic number comparison in children with and without dyscalculia|journal=Cognition|date=2010|volume=115|issue=1|pages=10–25|doi=10.1016/j.cognition.2009.10.006|pmid=20149355|s2cid=24436798|doi-access=free}}</ref>  For example, [[Gavin R. Price]] and colleagues found that children with developmental dyscalculia showed no differential distance effect on reaction time relative to typically developing children, but they did show a greater effect of distance on response accuracy.<ref name=Price2007>{{cite journal|last1=Price|first1=G. R.|last2=Holloway|first2=I.|last3=Räsänen|first3=P.|last4=Vesterinen|first4=M.|last5=Ansari|first5=D.|title=Impaired parietal magnitude processing in developmental dyscalculia|journal=Current Biology|date=2007|volume=17|issue=24|pages=1042–1043|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2007.10.013|pmid=18088583|s2cid=5673579|doi-access=free|bibcode=2007CBio...17R1042P }}</ref>

They also found that the right [[intraparietal sulcus]] in children with developmental dyscalculia was not modulated to the same extent in response to non-symbolic numerical processing as in typically developing children.<ref name=Price2007/> With the robust implication of the intraparietal sulcus in magnitude representation, it is possible that children with developmental dyscalculia have a weak magnitude representation in the parietal region. It does not rule out an impaired ability to access and manipulate numerical quantities from their symbolic representations (e.g., Arabic digits).<ref name=Price2007/>

Findings from a cross-sectional study suggest that children with developmental dyscalculia might have a delayed development in their numerical magnitude representation by as much as five years.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Piazza|first1=M.|last2=Facoetti|first2=A.|last3=Trussardi|first3=A. N.|last4=Berteletti|first4=I.|last5=Conte|first5=S.|last6=Lucangeli|first6=D.|last7=Dehaene|first7=S.|last8=Zorzi|first8=M.|title=Developmental trajectory of number acuity reveals a severe impairment in developmental dyscalculia|journal=Cognition|date=2010|volume=116|issue=1|pages=33–41|doi=10.1016/j.cognition.2010.03.012|pmid=20381023|s2cid=15878244}}</ref> The lack of longitudinal studies still leaves the question open as to whether the deficient numerical magnitude representation is a delayed development or impairment.{{citation needed|date=July 2021}}

===Access deficit hypothesis===

Rousselle & Noël propose that dyscalculia is caused by the inability to map preexisting representations of numerical magnitude onto symbolic Arabic digits.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rousselle|first1=L.|last2=Noel|first2=M.P.|title=Basic numerical skills in children with mathematics learning disabilities: A comparison of symbolic vs. non-symbolic number magnitude|journal=Cognition|date=2007|volume=102|issue=3|pages=361–395|doi=10.1016/j.cognition.2006.01.005|pmid=16488405|s2cid=8623796}}</ref> Evidence for this hypothesis is based on research studies that have found that individuals with dyscalculia are proficient on tasks that measure knowledge of non-symbolic numerical magnitude (i.e., non-symbolic comparison tasks) but show an impaired ability to process symbolic representations of number (i.e., symbolic comparison tasks).<ref>{{cite journal|last1=De Smedt|first1=B.|last2=Gilmore|first2=C.K.|title=Defective number module or impaired access? Numerical magnitude processing in first graders with mathematical difficulties|journal=Journal of Experimental Child Psychology|date=2011|volume=108|issue=2|pages=278–292|doi=10.1016/j.jecp.2010.09.003|pmid=20974477|s2cid=3557923 |url=https://dspace.lboro.ac.uk/2134/8764}}</ref>

[[Neuroimaging|Neuroimaging studies]] also report increased activation in the right [[intraparietal sulcus]] during tasks that measure symbolic but not non-symbolic processing of numerical magnitude.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Mussolin|first1=C.|last2=De Volder|first2=A.|last3=Grandin|first3=C.|last4=Schlögel|first4=X.|last5=Nassogne|first5=M.C.|last6=Noël|first6=M.P.|title=Neural correlates of symbolic number comparison in developmental dyscalculia|journal=Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience|date=2010|volume=22|issue=5|pages=860–874|doi=10.1162/jocn.2009.21237|pmid=19366284|hdl=2078.1/22220|s2cid=20157296|hdl-access=free}}</ref> However, support for the access deficit hypothesis is not consistent across research studies.<ref name=Price2007/>

==Diagnosis==
[[File:Examples of the numerical stroop effect trials.jpg|thumb|305x305px|The example of each condition in the [[numerical Stroop effect]] task]]
At its most basic level, dyscalculia is a learning disability affecting the normal development of arithmetic skills.<ref>{{cite journal|last2=Shalev|first2=Ruth|title=Number development and developmental dyscalculia|journal=Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology|date=2007|volume=49|issue=11|pages=868–873|doi=10.1111/j.1469-8749.2007.00868.x|pmid=17979867|s2cid=17349611|doi-access=free|last1=Von Aster|first1= Michael G}}</ref> A consensus has not yet been reached on appropriate diagnostic criteria for dyscalculia.<ref name="Berch">{{cite book|last1=Berch, Mozacco|title=Why Is Math So Hard for Some Children? The Nature and Origins of Mathematical Learning Difficulties and Disabilities|publisher=Brookes Publishing Company|date=2007|pages=[https://archive.org/details/whyismathsohardf0000unse/page/416 416]|url=https://archive.org/details/whyismathsohardf0000unse/page/416|isbn=978-1-55766-864-6}}</ref> Mathematics is a specific domain that is complex (i.e. includes many different processes, such as arithmetic, algebra, word problems, geometry, etc.) and cumulative (i.e. the processes build on each other such that mastery of an advanced skill requires mastery of many basic skills).{{citation needed|date=September 2026}}

Thus dyscalculia can be diagnosed using different criteria, and frequently is. This variety in diagnostic criteria leads to variability in identified samples, and thus variability in research findings regarding dyscalculia.{{citation needed|date=July 2021}}

Other than using achievement tests as diagnostic criteria, researchers often rely on domain-specific tests (i.e. tests of working memory, executive function, inhibition, intelligence, etc.) and teacher evaluations to create a more comprehensive diagnosis. Alternatively, fMRI research has shown that the brains of the children not affected can be reliably distinguished from the brains of the dyscalculic children based on the activation in the prefrontal cortex.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Dinkel|title=Diagnosing Developmental Dyscalculia on the Basis of Reliable Single Case FMRI Methods: Promises and Limitations|journal=PLOS ONE|date=2013|volume=8|issue=12|doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0083722|bibcode = 2013PLoSO...883722D|article-number=e83722|pmid=24349547|pmc=3857322|doi-access=free}}</ref> Due to the cost and time limitations associated with brain and neural research, these methods would likely not be incorporated into diagnostic criteria despite their effectiveness.{{citation needed|date=July 2021}}

===Types===
Research on subtypes of dyscalculia has begun without consensus; preliminary research has focused on comorbid learning disorders as subtyping candidates. The most common [[comorbidity]] in individuals with dyscalculia is dyslexia.<ref name="LanderlEtal04" /> Most studies done with comorbid samples versus dyscalculic-only samples have shown different mechanisms at work and additive effects of comorbidity, indicating that such subtyping may not be helpful in diagnosing dyscalculia. But there is variability in results at present.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Landerl|title=Dyslexia and dyscalculia: Two learning disorders with different cognitive profiles|journal=Journal of Experimental Child Psychology|date=2009|volume=103|issue=3|pages=309–324|pmid=19398112|last2=Fussenegger |first2=B|last3=Moll |first3=K |last4= Willburger|first4=E|doi=10.1016/j.jecp.2009.03.006}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rouselle|last2=Noël|title=Basic numerical skills in children with mathematics learning disabilities: A comparison of symbolic vs non-symbolic number magnitude processing|journal=Cognition|date=2007|volume=102|issue=3|pages=361–395|pmid=16488405|doi=10.1016/j.cognition.2006.01.005|s2cid=8623796}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1= Rosselli|first1=Monica|last2=Matute|first2=Esmeralda|last3=Pinto|first3=Noemi|last4=Ardila|first4=Alfredo|title=Memory Abilities in Children With Subtypes of Dyscalculia|journal=Developmental Neuropsychology |date=2006|volume=30|issue=3|pages=801–818|doi=10.1207/s15326942dn3003_3|pmid=17083294|s2cid=710722}}</ref>

Due to high comorbidity with other disabilities such as dyslexia,<ref name="LanderlEtal04">{{cite journal|last1=Landerl|first1=K|last2=Bevan|first2=A|last3=Butterworth|first3=B|title=Developmental dyscalculia and basic numerical capacities: a study of 8-9-year-old students|journal=Cognition|date=2004|volume=93|issue=2|pages=99–125|doi=10.1016/j.cognition.2003.11.004|pmid=15147931|s2cid=14205159}}</ref> or [[ADHD]],<ref name="Shalev">{{cite journal|last1=Shalev|first1=R|title=Developmental Dyscalculia|journal=Journal of Child Neurology|date=2004|volume=19|issue=10|pages=765–771|pmid=15559892|doi=10.1177/08830738040190100601|s2cid=4485310}}</ref> some researchers have suggested the possibility of subtypes of mathematical disabilities with different underlying profiles and causes.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Geary|first1=DC|title=Mathematical disabilities: Cognitive, neuropsychological, and genetic components|journal=Psychological Bulletin|date=1993|volume=114|issue=2|pages=345–362|doi=10.1037/0033-2909.114.2.345|pmid=8416036}}</ref><ref name="Rubinsten2009">{{cite journal |last1=Rubinsten |first1= O |last2= Henik |first2= A |title=Developmental dyscalculia: Heterogeneity might not mean different mechanisms |journal=Trends Cogn. Sci. (Regul. Ed.) |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=92–9 |date=February 2009 |pmid=19138550 |doi=10.1016/j.tics.2008.11.002 |s2cid= 205394589 }}</ref> Whether a particular subtype is specifically termed "dyscalculia" as opposed to a more general mathematical learning disability is somewhat under debate in the [[scientific literature]].
* '''Semantic memory''': This subtype often coexists with reading disabilities such as [[dyslexia]] and is characterized by poor representation and retrieval from [[long-term memory]]. These processes share a common [[neural pathway]] in the left [[angular gyrus]], which has been shown to be selective in arithmetic fact retrieval strategies,<ref name=GrabnerEtal09>{{cite journal|last1=Grabner|first1=RH|last2=Ansari|first2=D|last3=Koschutnig|first3=K|last4=Reishofer|first4=G|last5=Ebner|first5=F|last6=Neuper|first6=C|title=To retrieve or to calculate? Left angular gyrus mediates the retrieval of arithmetic facts during problem solving|journal=Neuropsychologia|date=2009|volume=47|issue=2|pages=604–608|doi=10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2008.10.013|pmid=19007800|s2cid=11149677}}</ref> as well as symbolic magnitude judgments.<ref name=HollowayEtal10>{{cite journal|last1=Holloway|first1=ID|last2=Price|first2=GR|last3=Ansari|first3=D|title=Common and segregated neural pathways for the processing of symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical magnitude: An fMRI study|journal=NeuroImage|date=2010|volume=49|issue=1|pages=1006–1017|doi=10.1016/j.neuroimage.2009.07.071|pmid=19666127|s2cid=11282288}}</ref> This region also shows low functional connectivity with language-related areas during phonological processing in adults with dyslexia.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Horwitz|first1=B|last2=Rumsey|first2=JM|last3=Donohue|first3=BC|title=Functional connectivity of the angular gyrus in normal reading and dyslexia|journal=PNAS|date=1998|volume=95|issue=15|pages=8939–8944|bibcode=1998PNAS...95.8939H|doi=10.1073/pnas.95.15.8939|pmid=9671783|pmc=21181|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=PughEtal00>{{cite journal|last1=Pugh|first1=KR|last2=Mencl|first2=WE|last3=Shaywitz|first3=BA|last4=Shaywitz|first4=SE|last5=Fulbright|first5=RK|last6=Constable|first6=RT|last7=Skudlarski|first7=P|last8=Marchione|first8=KE|last9=Jenner|first9=AR|last10=Fletcher|first10=JM|last11=Liberman|first11=AM|last12=Shakweiler|first12=DP|last13=Katz|first13=L|last14=Lacadie|first14=C|last15=Gore|first15=JC|title=The Angluar Gyrus in Developmental Dyslexia: Task-Specific Differences in Functional Connectivity With Posterior Cortex|journal=Psychological Science|date=2000|volume=11|issue=1|pages=51–56|doi=10.1111/1467-9280.00214|pmid=11228843|s2cid=12792506}}</ref> Thus, disruption to the left angular gyrus can cause both reading impairments and difficulties in calculation. This has been observed in individuals with [[Gerstmann syndrome]], of which dyscalculia is one of constellation of symptoms.
* '''Procedural concepts''': Research by Geary has shown that in addition to increased problems with fact retrieval, children with mathematical disabilities may rely on immature computational strategies. Specifically, children with mathematical disabilities showed poor command of counting strategies unrelated to their ability to retrieve numeric facts.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Geary|first1=DC|title=A componential analysis of an early learning deficit in mathematics|journal=Journal of Experimental Child Psychology|date=1990|volume=49|issue=3|pages=363–383|doi=10.1016/0022-0965(90)90065-G|pmid=2348157}}</ref> This research notes that it is difficult to discern whether poor conceptual knowledge is indicative of a qualitative deficit in number processing or simply a delay in typical mathematical development.
* '''Working memory''': Studies have found that children with dyscalculia showed impaired performance on [[working memory]] tasks compared to non affected children.<ref name=McLeanHitch99>{{cite journal|last1=McLean|first1=JF|last2=Hitch|first2=GJ|title=Working Memory Impairments in Children with Specific Arithmetic Learning Difficulties|journal=Journal of Experimental Child Psychology|date=1999|volume=74|issue=3|pages=240–260|doi=10.1006/jecp.1999.2516|pmid=10527556}}</ref><ref name=SzucsEtal13>{{cite journal|last1=Szucs|first1=D|last2=Devine|first2=A|last3=Soltesz|first3=F|last4=Nobes|first4=A|last5=Gabriel|first5=F|title=Developmental dyscalculia is related to visuo-spatial memory and inhibition impairment|journal=Cortex|date=2013|volume=49|issue=10|pages=2674–2688|doi=10.1016/j.cortex.2013.06.007|pmid=23890692|pmc=3878850}}</ref> Furthermore, research has shown that children with dyscalculia have weaker activation of the [[intraparietal sulcus]] during visuospatial working memory tasks.<ref name=":1">{{cite journal|last1=Rotzer|first1=S|last2=Loenneker|first2=T|last3=Kucian|first3=K|last4=Martin|first4=E|last5=Klaver|first5=P|last6=von Aster|first6=M|title=Dysfunctional neural network of spatial working memory contributes to developmental dyscalculia|journal=Neuropsychologia|date=2009|volume=47|issue=13|pages=2859–2865|doi=10.1016/j.neuropsychologia.2009.06.009|pmid=19540861|s2cid=35077903|url=http://www.zora.uzh.ch/id/eprint/20441/1/Rotzer_manuscript_V.pdf|access-date=31 December 2018|archive-date=23 January 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200123181733/https://www.zora.uzh.ch/id/eprint/20441/1/Rotzer_manuscript_V.pdf}}</ref> Brain activity in this region during such tasks has been linked to overall arithmetic performance,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Dumontheil|first1=I|last2=Klingberg|first2=T|title=Brain Activity during a Visuospatial Working Memory Task Predicts Arithmetical Performance 2 Years Later|journal=Cerebral Cortex|date=2012|volume=22|issue=5|pages=1078–1085|doi=10.1093/cercor/bhr175|pmid=21768226|doi-access=free}}</ref> indicating that numerical and working memory functions may converge in the intraparietal sulcus; however, working memory problems are confounded with domain-general learning difficulties, thus these deficits may not be specific to dyscalculia but rather may reflect a greater learning deficit. Dysfunction in prefrontal regions may also lead to deficits in working memory and other executive function, accounting for comorbidity with ADHD.<ref name=Shalev /><ref name=Rubinsten2009 />

Although evidence is not yet concrete, studies have shown indications of causes due to [[congenital]] or [[hereditary disorder]]s.<ref name="pmid15727331">{{cite journal |last1=Monuteaux |first1= MC |last2= Faraone |first2= SV |last3= Herzig |first3= K |last4= Navsaria |first4= N |last5= Biederman |first5= J |title=ADHD and dyscalculia: Evidence for independent familial transmission |journal=J Learn Disabil |volume=38 |issue=1 |pages=86–93 |year=2005 |pmid=15727331 |doi= 10.1177/00222194050380010701|s2cid= 10702955 }}</ref>

==Treatment==
To date, very few interventions have been developed specifically for individuals with dyscalculia. Concrete manipulation activities have been used for decades to train basic number concepts for remediation purposes.<ref>{{cite book |author1=A. Anning |author2=A. Edwards |title=Promoting Children's Learning from Birth to Five: Developing the New Early Years Professional|publisher=Open University Press|location=Maidenhead, UK|year=1999}}</ref> This method facilitates the intrinsic relationship between a goal, the learner's action, and the informational feedback on the action.<ref>{{cite book|author=S. Papert|title=Mindstorms: Children, Computers, and Powerful Ideas |publisher=Harvester Press |location=Brighton, UK |date=1980}}</ref><ref name="Butterworth, B. 2011">{{cite journal|vauthors=Butterworth B, Varma S, Laurillard D |year=2011 |title=Dyscalculia: from brain to education |journal=Science |volume=332 |issue=6033 |pages=1049–53|doi=10.1126/science.1201536|pmid=21617068|bibcode=2011Sci...332.1049B|s2cid=13311738 }}</ref> A one-to-one tutoring paradigm designed by [[Lynn Fuchs]] and colleagues which teaches concepts in arithmetic, number concepts, counting, and number families using games, flash cards, and manipulables has proven successful in children with generalized math learning difficulties, but intervention has yet to be tested specifically on children with dyscalculia.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Fuchs LS|author2=Powell SR|author3=Hamlett CL|author4=Fuchs D|year=2008|title=Remediating computational deficits at third grade: A randomized field trial|journal=Journal of Research on Educational Effectiveness|volume=1|issue=1|pages=2–32| pmc=3121170|doi=10.1080/19345740701692449|pmid=21709759}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Fuchs LS |author2=Geary DC |author3=Compton DL |author4=Fuchs D|author5=Schatschneider C|author6=Hamlett CL|author7=Deselms J|author8=Seethaler PM|author9=Wilson J|author10=Craddock CF|author11=Bryant JD|author12=Luther K|author13=Changas P |title=Effects of first-grade number knowledge tutoring with contrasting forms of practice|journal=Journal of Educational Psychology |issue=1|pages=58–77|pmid=24065865|doi=10.1037/a0030127|volume=105|date=Jan 2013|pmc=3779611}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|vauthors=Powell SR, Fuchs LS, Fuchs D, Cirino PT, Fletcher JM|year=2009|title=Effects of fact retrieval tutoring on third-grade students with math difficulties with and without reading difficulties|journal=Learning Disabilities Research and Practice|volume=24|issue=1|pages=1–11|pmc=2682421|doi=10.1111/j.1540-5826.2008.01272.x|pmid=19448840}}</ref>

These methods require specially trained teachers working directly with small groups or individual students. As such, instruction time in the classroom is necessarily limited. For this reason, several research groups have developed computer adaptive training programs designed to target deficits unique to dyscalculic individuals.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-10-05 |title=Dynamo Intervention |url=https://dynamomaths.co.uk/dynamo-maths/dynamo-intervention/ |access-date=2023-08-29 |website=Dynamo Maths |language=en-GB}}</ref>

Software intended to remediate dyscalculia has been developed.<ref name="=Wilson, 2006">{{cite journal |vauthors=Wilson AJ, Revkin SK, Cohen D, Cohen L, Dehaene S|title=An open trial assessment of "The Number Race", an adaptive computer game for remediation of dyscalculia |journal=Behav Brain Funct |volume=2 |page=20 |year=2006 |pmid=16734906 |pmc=1523349 |doi=10.1186/1744-9081-2-20 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Apps to Help Students With Dyscalculia and Math Difficulties|url=http://www.ncld.org/students-disabilities/assistive-technology-education/apps-students-ld-dyscalculia-math-difficulties|publisher=National Center for Learning Disabilities and Math Difficulties|author1=Hatton, Darla|author2=Hatton, Kaila|access-date=26 March 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130121013152/http://www.ncld.org/students-disabilities/assistive-technology-education/apps-students-ld-dyscalculia-math-difficulties|archive-date=21 January 2013}}</ref><ref name=pmid23302840/> While computer adaptive training programs are modeled after one-to-one type interventions, they provide several advantages. Most notably, individuals are able to practice more with a digital intervention than is typically possible with a class or teacher.<ref name="Butterworth, B. 2010">{{cite journal |vauthors=Butterworth B, Laurillard D |year=2010 |title=Low numeracy and dyscalculia: identification and intervention|journal=ZDM|volume=42|issue=6|pages=527–539|doi=10.1007/s11858-010-0267-4|s2cid=2566749 }}</ref> As with one-to-one interventions, several digital interventions have also proven successful in children with generalized math learning difficulties. Räsänen and colleagues have found that games such as ''The Number Race'' and ''Graphogame-math'' can improve performance on number comparison tasks in children with generalized math learning difficulties.<ref name="Kucian, K. 2011">{{cite journal |vauthors=Kucian K, Grond U, Rotzer S, Henzi B, Schönmann C, Plangger F, Gälli M, Martin E, von Aster M |year=2011|title=Mental number line training in children with developmental dyscalculia|journal=NeuroImage|volume=57|issue=3|pages=782–795|doi=10.1016/j.neuroimage.2011.01.070|pmid=21295145|s2cid=12098609}}</ref><ref name="Räsänen, P.">{{cite journal |vauthors=Räsänen P, Salminen J, Wilson AJ, Aunio P, Dehaene S |year=2009|title=Computer-assisted intervention for children with low numeracy skills|journal=Cognitive Development|volume=24|issue=4|pages=450–472 |doi=10.1016/j.cogdev.2009.09.003}}</ref>

Several digital interventions have been developed for dyscalculics specifically. Each attempts to target basic processes that are associated with maths difficulties. Rescue Calcularis was one early computerized intervention that sought to improve the integrity of and access to the mental number line.<ref name="Kucian, K. 2011"/> Other digital interventions for dyscalculia adapt games, flash cards, and manipulables to function through technology.<ref name="Butterworth, B. 2010"/> While each intervention claims to improve basic numerosity skills, the authors of these interventions do admit that repetition and practice effects may be a factor involved in reported performance gains.<ref name="Butterworth, B. 2010" /><ref name="Kucian, K. 2011" /><ref name="Räsänen, P." />

An additional criticism is that these digital interventions lack the option to manipulate numerical quantities.<ref name="Butterworth, B. 2011" /> While the previous two games provide the correct answer, the individual using the intervention cannot actively determine, through manipulation, what the correct answer should be. Butterworth and colleagues argued that games like The Number Bonds, which allows an individual to compare different sized rods, should be the direction that digital interventions move toward. Such games use manipulation activities to provide intrinsic motivation toward content guided by dyscalculia research. One of these [[serious game]]s is [[Meister Cody – Talasia]], an online training that includes the [[CODY Assessment]] – a diagnostic test for detecting dyscalculia. Based on these findings, Dybuster Calcularis was extended by adaptation algorithms and game forms allowing manipulation by the learners.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Käser|first1=Tanja|last2=Baschera|first2=Gian-Marco|last3=Kohn|first3=Juliane|last4=Kucian|first4=Karin|last5=Richtmann|first5=Verena|last6=Grond|first6=Ursina|last7=Gross|first7=Markus|last8=von Aster|first8=Michael|date=2013-01-01|title=Design and evaluation of the computer-based training program Calcularis for enhancing numerical cognition|journal= Frontiers in Psychology|volume=4|page=489|doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2013.00489|pmc=3733013|pmid=23935586|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rauscher|first1=Larissa|last2=Kohn|first2=Juliane|last3=Käser|first3=Tanja|last4=Mayer|first4=Verena|last5=Kucian|first5=Karin|last6=McCaskey|first6=Ursina|last7=Esser|first7=Günter|last8=von Aster|first8=Michael|date=2016-01-01|title=Evaluation of a Computer-Based Training Program for Enhancing Arithmetic Skills and Spatial Number Representation in Primary School Children|journal= Frontiers in Psychology|page=913|doi=10.3389/fpsyg.2016.00913|pmc=4921479|pmid=27445889|volume=7|doi-access=free}}</ref> It was found to improve addition, subtraction and number line tasks, and was made available as [[Dybuster#Dybuster Calcularis|Dybuster Calcularis]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Käser|first1=T.|last2=Busetto|first2=A. G.|last3=Solenthaler|first3=B.|last4=Baschera|first4=G.-M.|last5=Kohn|first5=J.|last6=Kucian|first6=K.|last7=von Aster|first7=M.|last8=Gross|first8=M.|year=2013|title=Modelling and Optimizing Mathematics Learning in Children|url=https://cgl.ethz.ch/publications/papers/paperKae13d.php|journal=International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education|volume=23 |issue=1–4|pages=115–135|doi=10.1007/s40593-013-0003-7|s2cid=2528111|doi-access=free|hdl=20.500.11850/74824|hdl-access=free}}</ref>

A study used [[transcranial direct current stimulation]] (tDCS) to the parietal lobe during numerical learning and demonstrated selective improvement of numerical abilities that was still present six months later in typically developing individuals.<ref name="Cohen, 2010">{{cite journal|last1=Cohen Kadosh|first1=R |last2=Soskic |first2=S |last3=Iuculano|first3=T |last4=Kanai|first4=R |last5=Walsh|first5=V |title=Modulating neuronal activity produces specific and long-lasting changes in numerical competence|journal=Current Biology|volume=20|issue=22|year=2010|pages=2016–2020|issn=0960-9822|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2010.10.007 |pmid=21055945 |pmc=2990865|bibcode=2010CBio...20.2016C }}</ref> Improvement were achieved by applying anodal current to the right parietal lobe and cathodal current to the left parietal lobe and contrasting it with the reverse setup. When the same research group used tDCS in a training study with two dyscalculic individuals, the reverse setup (left anodal, right cathodal) demonstrated improvement of numerical abilities.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Iuculano T, Cohen Kadosh R |year=2014|title=Preliminary evidence for performance enhancement following parietal lobe stimulation in Developmental Dyscalculia|journal=Frontiers in Human Neuroscience |volume=8 |page=38 |doi=10.3389/fnhum.2014.00038 |pmid=24570659|pmc=3916771|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Epidemiology==
Dyscalculia is thought to be present in 3–6% of the general population, but estimates by country and sample vary somewhat.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Shalev |first1 = Ruth S|title=Developmental dyscalculia |journal= Pediatric Neurology|date=2001|volume=24|issue=5|pages=337–342|url=http://www.pedneur.com/article/S0887-8994(00)00258-7/abstract|pmid=11516606|last2=Gross-Tsur|first2=V|doi=10.1016/s0887-8994(00)00258-7}}</ref> Many studies have found prevalence rates by gender to be equivalent.<ref name="Berch" /><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Gross-Tsur|first1=Varda|title=Developmental Dyscalculia: Prevalence and Demographic Features |last2=Manor|first2=Orly|last3=Shalev|first3=Ruth S.|journal=Developmental Medicine and Child Neurology|date=1996|volume=38|issue=1|pages=25–33|doi=10.1111/j.1469-8749.1996.tb15029.x |pmid= 8606013 |s2cid= 45328920}}</ref> Those that find gender difference in prevalence rates often find dyscalculia higher in females, but some few studies have found prevalence rates higher in males.<ref name= pmid25529864/>

== History ==
The term ''dyscalculia'' was coined in the 1940s, but it was not completely recognized until 1974 by the work of Slovak researcher Ladislav Košč. Košč defined dyscalculia as "a structural disorder of mathematical abilities". His research proved that the learning disability was caused by impairments to certain parts of the brain that control mathematical calculations and not because symptomatic individuals were "mentally handicapped". Researchers now sometimes use the terms "math dyslexia" or "math learning disability" when they mention the condition.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Whitney |first=A. K. |date=2015-04-06 |title=11 Facts About the Math Disorder Dyscalculia |work=[[Mental Floss]] |url=http://mentalfloss.com/article/62436/11-facts-about-math-disorder-dyscalculia |access-date=2018-04-25}}</ref>

Cognitive disabilities specific to mathematics were originally identified in case studies with patients who experienced specific arithmetic disabilities as a result of damage to specific regions of the brain.  More commonly, dyscalculia occurs developmentally as a genetically linked learning disability which affects a person's ability to understand, remember, or manipulate numbers or number facts (e.g., the [[multiplication table]]s). The term is often used to refer specifically to the inability to perform arithmetic operations, but is also defined by some educational professionals and [[Cognitive psychology|cognitive psychologists]] such as [[Stanislas Dehaene]],<ref name="Dehaene1997">{{cite book|title=The Number Sense: How the Mind Creates Mathematics|url=https://archive.org/details/numbersensehowmi0000deha|url-access=registration|last=Dehaene|first=S.|publisher=[[Oxford University Press]]|year=1997|isbn=978-0-19-513240-3|location=New York}}</ref> or [[Brian Butterworth]],<ref name="Butterworth, 2011" /> as a more fundamental inability to conceptualize numbers as abstract concepts of comparative quantities (a deficit in "[[number sense]]"), which these researchers consider to be a foundational skill upon which other mathematics abilities build.

Symptoms of dyscalculia include the delay of simple counting, inability to memorize simple arithmetic facts such as adding, subtracting, etc. There are few known symptoms because little research has been done on the topic.<ref name="Butterworth, 2010" /><ref name="Butterworth, 2011" />

==Etymology==
{{distinguish|Discalced}}
The term ''dyscalculia'' dates back to at least 1949.<ref name="Pollak2009">{{cite book|last=Trott |first=Clare |editor-first=David |editor-last= Pollak|title=Neurodiversity in Higher Education: Positive Responses to Specific Learning Differences |chapter=Dyscalculia|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eVhQoqboi1UC&pg=PA125 |date=5 March 2009|publisher=John Wiley and Sons|isbn=978-0-470-99753-6}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Košč|first=Ladislav |year=1974 |title=Developmental dyscalculia |journal=Journal of Learning Disabilities |volume=7 |number=3 |pages=159–62 |doi=10.1177/002221947400700309|s2cid=220679067}}</ref> Dyscalculia comes from [[Greek language|Greek]] and [[Latin]] and means "counting badly". The prefix {{Lang|grc-latn|dys-}} comes from Greek and means "badly". The root ''calculia'' comes from the Latin {{Lang|la|calculare}}, which means "[[counting|to count]]"; it is also a [[cognate]] of ''[[calculation]]'' and ''[[calculus]]''.
